summary: Specifies how a Mobile IPv6 home agent talks to a Diameter server run by the mobile service provider. This lets deployments handle authentication, authorization and configuration dynamically, whether the mobile node authenticates using IKEv2 with EAP or using the Mobile IPv6 authentication protocol. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: When you move to a new place but keep your old address for mail, a helper at the post office checks with the main office that you are really you and lets your mail follow you.

questions: diameter and mobile ipv6 home agent
how does a home agent authenticate with diameter
how does a home agent talk to a diameter server
subtitle: How a Mobile IPv6 home agent asks a Diameter server to authenticate, authorize and account for a mobile node.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 home agent needs to know that a mobile node is allowed to use the service, and needs its home address and keys, without every deployment inventing its own way to ask the operator's AAA system.
tldr.mechanism: The home agent acts as a Diameter client. For IKEv2 with EAP it reuses the Diameter EAP commands (DER and DEA), and for the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol it uses two new commands, MIP6-Request and MIP6-Answer, with added AVPs that carry the bootstrapping data.
tldr.outcome: It defines two new Diameter applications, MIP6I (7) and MIP6A (8), plus session management and accounting rules. It is a Proposed Standard, and it leaves the actual session key derivation to each deployment.

today: RFC 5778 is a Proposed Standard from February 2010. No obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it, so it remains the definition of the home agent to Diameter server interaction it describes.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6, a mobile node (MN) owns a home address and has a home agent (HA). The MN registers with the HA so it can still be reached when it is away from its home link. That registration may need IPsec security associations and keying material, or it may be protected by a mobility message authentication option instead. Providing the home address, the HA address and the keys is called the Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping problem.

This RFC supplies the Diameter side of the answer. The mobility service provider wants to be sure the MN is authenticated, authorized and accounted for before any parameters are handed out. So the HA takes part in authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) through the provider's Diameter infrastructure. The document covers four functions: authentication, authorization, accounting and session management.

It is limited to two MN authentication methods: IKEv2 with EAP, and the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol from RFC 4285. New methods can be added by separate specifications.
sections.eli5: A traveling kid wants to keep getting letters at the old house. Before the helper forwards anything, the helper checks with the head office that the kid is allowed to use the service.

sections.title: Architecture and Application Identifiers
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows three parties. The MN talks to the HA with a front-end protocol, either IKEv2 or the protocol of RFC 4285. The HA also acts as a Diameter client and talks to the Diameter server (the home AAA server, or AAAH, in the user's home realm) over the back-end protocol that this document defines.

The RFC defines two new Diameter applications:

  • MIP6I (Diameter Mobile IPv6 IKE), Application Identifier 7, used when the MN is authenticated and authorized using IKEv2.
  • MIP6A (Diameter Mobile IPv6 Auth), Application Identifier 8, used when the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol is used.

Accounting is a separate choice. In the coupled model accounting messages carry the MIP6I or MIP6A identifier. In the split model they use the Diameter Base Accounting identifier, value 3.
sections.eli5: There are two different forms at the head office, one for people who show a special ID card and one for people who use a secret handshake. Each form has its own number so the clerks know which one it is.

sections.title: Authenticating the Mobile Node
sections.content:
IKEv2 with EAP. The MN and HA start with an IKE_SA_INIT exchange to negotiate algorithms and swap nonces and Diffie-Hellman values. In the first IKE_AUTH message the MN leaves out the AUTH field to show it wants EAP, and it may use a CFG_REQUEST payload to ask for or suggest a home address or home prefix. The HA pulls the identity out of the IDi field and sends a Diameter-EAP-Request (DER) to the Diameter server, with an EAP-Response/Identity inside. The server chooses the EAP method and answers with Diameter-EAP-Answer (DEA) messages. The Diameter EAP logic of RFC 4072 is reused as it is. EAP methods that do not establish a shared key SHOULD NOT be used, because of man-in-the-middle attacks.

Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol. Here a Binding Update (BU) arriving at the HA triggers a MIP6-Request to the Diameter server, and the server replies with a MIP6-Answer. The HA copies the value of the MN-NAI mobility option into the User-Name AVP. This exchange is only needed for the first BU, when the HA has no security association yet; later BUs are handled locally, though the HA MAY re-authorize the MN at any time. The RFC assumes the MN-AAA option is present in the BU and that the Diameter server computes the session keys, but how it does that is out of scope.

In both cases it is RECOMMENDED that the HA sends an accounting request every time it receives a BU. If the HA also serves conventional IPsec VPN access, one approach already supported by IKEv2 is to use different responder identities for the two roles.
sections.eli5: Either the kid shows an ID card to the helper, who phones the head office, or the kid sends a sealed note that the head office checks. In both cases the helper only lets the mail follow the kid after the head office says yes.

sections.title: Commands and AVPs
sections.content:
For IKEv2 with EAP the RFC reuses the Diameter EAP commands DER and DEA, both with command code 268, and adds Mobile IPv6 AVPs to their definitions. The DER must set Application-ID to 7 and the Auth-Request-Type AVP to AUTHORIZE_AUTHENTICATE. The Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping AVPs appear only in the first DER and, on success, in the last DEA that carries EAP-Success.

For the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol it defines two new commands: MIP6-Request (MIR) and MIP6-Answer (MIA), both with command code 325. The MIR carries the MIP6-Auth-Mode AVP and, for the MN-AAA mode, the SPI, authenticator and mobility data taken from the BU. A MIA with DIAMETER_SUCCESS MUST include the MIP-Mobile-Node-Address AVP.

Notable AVPs include:

  • MIP-Mobile-Node-Address (333): the home address. If a request carries 0::0 or 0.0.0.0, the HA expects the server to assign one.
  • MIP6-Agent-Info (486): the HA address. With the result code DIAMETER_SUCCESS_RELOCATE_HA the server tells the HA it MUST start an HA switch.
  • MIP-MN-HA-MSA (492): a grouped AVP holding the session key, its lifetime and related data.
  • MIP6-Auth-Mode (494): the authentication mode; only MIP6_AUTH_MN_AAA is defined.

Two new result codes are added: DIAMETER_SUCCESS_RELOCATE_HA (2009) and DIAMETER_ERROR_MIP6_AUTH_MODE (5041), the latter for a mode the server does not support.
sections.eli5: The messages are forms with labeled boxes. Some boxes say who the kid is, some say where the kid is now, and some hold a secret key the helper will use.

sections.title: Session Management and Accounting
sections.content:
Each security association between the MN and HA created by a successful IKEv2 negotiation or Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol exchange corresponds to one Diameter session. The HA MUST support the Authorization Session State Machine of RFC 3588.

Either side can end the session early. The HA sends a Session-Termination-Request, and then MUST terminate the Mobile IPv6 binding and the SA. The Diameter server can send an Abort-Session-Request, and the HA MUST terminate the SA and then the binding.

The HA MUST also be able to act as a Diameter client that collects accounting records. The split accounting model, using Application Identifier 3, is the preferred choice because it permits centralized accounting for several applications. In the coupled model the accounting AVPs that SHOULD be included cover octet and packet counts in each direction, session time, the home address, the current care-of address and the Chargeable-User-Identity.
sections.eli5: If the head office says stop, or the kid says stop, the helper closes the forwarding and tells the other side. The helper also keeps count of how many letters were forwarded, like a meter.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated command code 325 for MIP6-Request/Answer, two Application Identifiers (7 for MIP6I and 8 for MIP6A), and the Result-Code values 2009 and 5041. It also registered new AVPs such as MIP-Careof-Address, MIP-Authenticator, MIP-MAC-Mobility-Data, MIP-Timestamp, MIP-MN-HA-SPI, MIP-MN-HA-MSA, Service-Selection and MIP6-Auth-Mode.

A new registry, the MIP6 Authentication Mode Registry, holds the values for MIP6-Auth-Mode. It starts with MIP6_AUTH_MN_AAA at value 1. New values need the Specification Required policy, and the value 0 is reserved.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new forms were written in the official number book, so nobody else uses the same ones by accident.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of RFC 5026, the Diameter base protocol and the Diameter EAP application. Messages may pass through AAA brokers or Diameter agents such as proxies, so HA-to-server communication depends on the security of those intermediaries.

For the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol the Diameter server derives the MN-HA security association and returns the session key to the HA. Neither this RFC nor other IETF specifications define how the server derives it. The overall security of the system therefore depends on how each deployment does that.
sections.eli5: The messages may pass through other offices on the way, so you have to trust them. And how the secret key is made is left for each post office to decide, so how safe it is depends on them.
